(b) [Smooth source fields] A **smooth (volume) source field** on
$\Omega\times I$ is a pair $(\rho,J)$ of maps $\rho:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$,
$J:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is continuous on $\Omega\times I$ and of
class $C^1$ wherever a displayed equation differentiates it; $\rho$ is the
**frame charge density** (C m$^{-3}$) and $J$ the **frame current density**
(A m$^{-2}$). For each fixed $t\in I$ retain the compact Jordan branch: if
$V\subseteq\Omega$ is compact and Jordan measurable, define

$$Q_R(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)dy$$

by [[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]], with integrability supplied by
[[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]. For the
full measurable-volume branch assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]),
as required by the published Lebesgue-measure interface. If $V$ is any bounded
Lebesgue-measurable subset with compact closure $\overline V\subseteq\Omega$,
define

$$Q(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)d\lambda_3(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}F_t(y)\mathbf{1}_V(y)d\lambda_3(y),$$

where $F_t=\rho(\cdot,t)$ on $\Omega$ and $0$ elsewhere; the signed integral is
defined through its positive and negative parts
([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]],
[[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]). The
function $F_t$ is Borel, and hence Lebesgue measurable: for every open
$O\subseteq\mathbb R$ its preimage inside the open set $\Omega$ is relatively
open in $\Omega$, hence open in $\mathbb R^3$, and the closed complement of
$\Omega$ is added precisely when $0\in O$
([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]],
[[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]). This integral is absolutely
finite: $\rho(\cdot,t)$ is bounded on the compact $\overline V$ by
[[thm-extreme-value-metric]], $V$ has finite Lebesgue measure by
[[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]], and the
monotonicity and homogeneity of the nonnegative integral
([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]) bound
$\int|F_t|\mathbf{1}_Vd\lambda_3\le M_t\lambda_3(V)<\infty$, the indicator
integral being its simple-function value
([[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]); the
positive and negative parts are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]. On
the compact Jordan branch, under the same Countable Choice assumption,
$Q=Q_R$ by [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]].
The
empty region has charge zero in both branches. The current flux remains
defined independently: for each oriented surface patch in $\Omega$ the current
flux at time $t$ is the surface integral of $J(\cdot,t)$ in the induced
orientation, as defined in [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]].
Point sources and sheet sources are not source fields in this sense; they are
different objects, defined by their own pairings when the framework uses them.

Adopt as a physical postulate of this framework the following four equations for
the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and the sources of [[def-em-sources]] on the
laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
$\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and the SI units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional
derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and let
$\rho,J$ be continuous. Then, with the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivative
$\partial_t$ at fixed position of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$

(b) [Weak branch] Let instead $E,B$ be locally integrable $\mathbb R^3$-valued
fields and $\rho,J$ locally integrable scalar and vector fields on
$I\times\Omega$, identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Let
$\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\partial_t$ act as
distributional derivatives, componentwise, and let $\psi$ range over
$C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).
Then the same four identities hold in the sense of [[def-distribution]]: the
pairings

$$\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$$

all vanish for every such $\psi$, all derivatives being distributional
derivatives ([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(c) [Scope] The postulate contains no magnetic charge: $\operatorname{div}B=0$
and no magnetic-source term appears in $\operatorname{curl}E$. Sources that
are not locally integrable functions (point or sheet sources) are covered by
neither branch and require their own definition. The equations are adopted
classical vacuum physics in the named inertial chart; they are not deduced from
charge conservation, from empirical agreement or from the special-relativity
postulates, and this item by itself asserts no covariance under changes of
inertial frame.

**Proper-graph branch.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, let $z:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be a $C^1$ trajectory, put $\gamma(t):=(z(t),t)$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ be open with $\gamma[I]\subseteq\Omega$. Assume the graph map $\gamma:I\to\Omega$ is **proper**: $\gamma^{-1}[K]$ is a compact subset of $I$ for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$. For $q\in\mathbb R$ and $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]) define

$$\langle\rho,\psi\rangle:=q\int_I\psi(z(t),t)\,dt,\qquad \langle J,\psi\rangle:=q\int_I z'(t)\,\psi(z(t),t)\,dt,$$

the second integral being componentwise, so $J=(J_1,J_2,J_3)$ is a triple of distributions, with components $\langle J_i,\psi\rangle=q\int_Iz_i'(t)\psi(z(t),t)\,dt$. Then $\rho$ and $J$ are distributions on $\Omega$ ([[def-distribution]]) and, with the distributional derivative of [[def-distributional-derivative]],

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0\qquad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\Omega).$$

Complex integrals mean $\int w:=\int\operatorname{Re}w+i\int\operatorname{Im}w$, with the same componentwise convention for improper limits. In formulas involving complex tests, $\langle u,w\rangle:=\sum_{j=1}^3u_jw_j$ for $u\in\mathbb R^3$ and $w\in\mathbb C^3$, with no conjugation. This extends the real coordinate pairing; estimates on $J$ mean estimates on each component.

In the proper branch, an integral over $I$ means the proper integral over any compact subinterval containing the pulled-back support, with the integrand zero near its ends; additivity makes this independent of the subinterval. For $I=\varnothing$ both functionals are defined to be zero. Properness is automatic if $\Omega=\mathbb R^3\times I$, and also if $I=\mathbb R$.

For $a\in\Omega$, the **Dirac distribution at $a$** is the complex-linear functional $\delta_a(\varphi)=\varphi(a)$ on $\mathcal D(\Omega)$, with the bilinear convention of [[def-distribution]]. It is continuous: the seminorm $q(\varphi)=|\varphi(a)|$ restricts on each $\mathcal D_K$ to a seminorm bounded by $p_0$ (and is zero if $a\notin K$), so it is one of the admissible seminorms defining the test topology.

Its derivatives are those of [[def-distributional-derivative]]:
$$\langle\partial^\alpha\delta_a,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\partial^\alpha\varphi(a).$$
They are distributions by that definition; on each fixed-support stage the absolute value is at most $p_{|\alpha|}(\varphi)$. If $a\notin K$ all derivatives of the test vanish at $a$, so the bound has zero left side. For $\alpha=0$ this is $\delta_a$; a first derivative evaluates the negative first derivative of the test. No conjugation and no choice are involved. On the empty open set there is no permitted point $a$, rather than a new Dirac distribution. The sharp order of these distributions requires a test witness and is proved in the assigned example later.

For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, write $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ when $f:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is Lebesgue measurable and $\int_K|f|<\infty$ for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$. This extends [[def-locally-integrable-function-on-r-n]]: equivalently, require integrability on every ball whose closure is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Such balls finitely cover each compact $K$, and conversely their closures are compact; on all of $\mathbb R^n$, any ball lies in a larger compact closed ball.

For a test $\varphi$ as in [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], define the **regular functional**

$$\langle u_f,\varphi\rangle=\int_\Omega f(x)\varphi(x)\,dx.$$

This is well-defined since $|\int f\varphi|\le\sup_K|\varphi|\int_K|f|$ for $K=\operatorname{supp}\varphi$. It is complex-linear in $f$ and in $\varphi$ and depends only on the almost-everywhere class of $f$. For an empty support the integral is zero. The subsequent embedding theorem establishes continuity, so that this is a distribution, and injectivity modulo almost-everywhere equality. That theorem states the Countable Choice cost of its injectivity proof; no choice is needed to define the displayed pairing.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The map $f\mapsto u_f$, $u_f(\varphi)=\int_\Omega f\varphi$, is a complex-linear injection from $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ modulo almost-everywhere equality into $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. It is continuous from the local $L^1$ topology, generated by $f\mapsto\int_K|f|$ for compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, to the strong distribution topology. In particular local $L^1$ convergence implies strong distribution convergence. The continuity estimate itself is choice-free; Countable Choice is used in the cited $L^1$ approximate-identity theorem proving injectivity.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Every at most countable subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-countable]]) is Lebesgue measurable with

$$\lambda_n(E) \;=\; 0,$$

so $E$ is a $\lambda_n$-null set ([[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]).
In particular every singleton is null, and on the real line the set
$\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ of rational reals ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]) satisfies
$\lambda_1(\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}) = 0$.

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

In a measure space $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ ([[def-measure-space]]), a measurable set $N\in\mathcal A$ is **$\mu$-null** if $\mu(N)=0$.

A property $P(x)$ holds **$\mu$-almost everywhere**, or **for $\mu$-almost every $x$**, if its exceptional set is contained in a measurable $\mu$-null set: there is $N\in\mathcal A$ with $\mu(N)=0$ such that $P(x)$ holds for every $x\in X\setminus N$. Both notions are relative to the named measure $\mu$.

In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$ open, there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Every open cover of $\Omega$ admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member. Subordination here asserts existence of such a member for each support; it does not select cover labels.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $Q=\prod_{i=1}^n[a_i,b_i]$ with $n\ge1$ and $a_i<b_i$. If a bounded Borel real function $f$ on $Q$ is Riemann integrable, then it is Lebesgue integrable and the two integrals agree. The corresponding assertion for complex functions holds componentwise. In particular it applies to smooth compact test integrands and their bounded Borel zero extensions from compact Jordan regions.

Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be bounded in the metric sense of
[[def-metric-bounded-diameter]] and Jordan measurable, and let
$f:E\to\mathbb R$ be bounded. Choose a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\supseteq E$, whose existence follows from
[[def-jordan-inner-and-outer-content]], and define the zero extension
$$\widetilde f_Q(x):=\begin{cases}f(x),&x\in E,\\0,&x\in Q\setminus E.\end{cases}$$
The function $f$ is **Riemann integrable over $E$** when $\widetilde f_Q$ is integrable over $Q$, and then
$$\int_Ef:=\int_Q\widetilde f_Q.$$
Independence of the bounding rectangle, for both integrability and value, is proved in [[lem-jordan-set-integral-well-defined]] and recorded as the definition's forward justification. For $f=1$, the zero extension is $1_E$, so [[thm-jordan-content-and-indicator-integrability]] gives $\int_E1=\operatorname{cont}(E)$.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable, and let $E\in\mathcal A$. Since
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]
implies that $f\chi_E$ is measurable, define the **integral of $f$ over $E$**
by
$$\int_E f\,d\mu:=\int f\chi_E\,d\mu,$$
where the integral on the right is the nonnegative Lebesgue integral of
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]].

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: For the smooth source $\rho=qf$, $J=0$: $\rho$ is $C^\infty$ with compact support and $J=0$ is smooth, so $(\rho,J)$ is a smooth source field in the sense of [F1]; for every bounded Lebesgue-measurable $V$ with compact closure in $\Omega$ containing $\operatorname{supp}f$ one has $f\mathbf 1_V=f$ pointwise, hence $Q(V,t)=\int_Vqf\,d\lambda_3=q\int_{\mathbb R^3}f\,d\lambda_3=q$ by [F11], and the same pair is therefore a source to which the smooth branch [F2] refers.

For the same $V$ required to be compact and Jordan measurable, the zero extension of $qf$ to a bounding rectangle is the bounded zero extension of a continuous function on a compact Jordan region, so it is Riemann integrable with $Q_R(V,t)=\int_Vqf=q$ by [F10]; thus both charge branches of [F1] give the same value $q$ on this source, as the definition of $\rho=qf$ predicts.

For the point source, the pairings of [F3] applied to the given proper trajectory define distributions on $\Omega\times I$ satisfying $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$; its fixed-time reading is the evaluation functional $q\delta_{z(t)}$ of [F4], in contrast with the fixed-time reading $\varphi\mapsto\int_\Omega\rho(y,t)\varphi(y)\,dy$ of a smooth-branch density.
For q=0 both the smooth functions and the point-source pairings are zero, hence give the same zero distributions.

Assume $q\ne0$ and suppose a locally integrable $\rho\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ satisfied $\langle\rho,\varphi\rangle=q\varphi(z_0)$ for every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$. Every test supported in the open set $\Omega\setminus\{z_0\}$ vanishes at $z_0$, so the regular distribution of $\rho|_{\Omega\setminus\{z_0\}}$ is zero; by injectivity [F6] this gives $\rho=0$ almost everywhere on $\Omega\setminus\{z_0\}$. The singleton $\{z_0\}$ is null by [F7], so their union is null by [F8] and $\rho=0$ almost everywhere on $\Omega$; since the regular distribution depends only on the almost-everywhere class [F5], $\langle\rho,\varphi_0\rangle=0$ for the cutoff $\varphi_0$ of [F9] with $\varphi_0=1$ on a neighborhood of the compact $\{z_0\}\subseteq\Omega$. But the assumed identity gives $\langle\rho,\varphi_0\rangle=q\varphi_0(z_0)=q\ne0$, a contradiction.

Both constructions carry total charge $q$ by steps 1.1-1.3. For $q\ne0$, step 2.1 proves that the point charge has no locally integrable representative, so it differs from the smooth density and is covered by neither Maxwell branch of [F2]'s postulate. For $q=0$, step 1.4 gives the common zero distributions. Only the point-source pairings and their continuity identity have been established, with no singular-source Maxwell adoption, field value at $z(t)$ or measurement.

boundaries.reason: No empty object occurs: the smooth density has unit total integral, the trajectory is defined on a nonempty open interval, and the point charge at a fixed time is a single event.

boundaries.evidence: Verification 2.1 explicitly assumes q != 0; 1.4 proves that q = 0 gives the common zero distributions. Conclusion 3.1 retains both cases.
Steps 1.1 and 1.2: the normalisation integral of f equals one and total charge q; the one-point set {z_0} is the singleton shown null in step 2.1.
A constant spatial trajectory is allowed; its spacetime graph is still proper in Omega x I. Verification 1.3 applies and 1.4 retains the zero-charge coincidence.
Step 1.2 and the fixed-time reading of step 1.3 hold at every time t in I, and the properness hypothesis of the trajectory supplier controls the endpoint behaviour of its integrals.

Countable Choice is carried through the measurable-volume/comparison branch and through the embedding injectivity and null-singleton suppliers in Verification 2.1; no additional choice principle is invoked.
